T:Mafuve
T:Dance of girls: Ndau dance song with four clap parts
C:traditional (Ndau), as sung by C. Kamba Simango
O:Mozambique (then Portuguese East Africa), Ndau people
R:dance song
S:Natalie Curtis Burlin, Songs and Tales from the Dark Continent (New York: G. Schirmer, 1920), "Mafuve: Dance of Girls", pp. 103-105 (words and dance pp. 29-30)
N:A dance song of Ndau girls and young women in central Mozambique, about a young bride who loves her new home but longs for her mother's: "Kwa-mai-we", my mother's home; "Kwa-mai nda le-ga", I left my mother's home; "Ndo da kwu-mi-sha", I love my husband's home; the rest are vocables. Two girls at a time dance facing each other in the middle, starting with two stamps; the others stand round in a circle, clapping and singing (Curtis, pp. 29-30, from C. Kamba Simango). Her 1920 book carries the colonial and racial language of its time in its title and commentary, so teach it as Simango's song, with the dance. No drums: the band plays Curtis's four printed hand-clap rhythms, each on its own sound so the layers can be told apart, and the dancers' two stamps; in class, four groups take one clap rhythm each and change every two or three bars, as Curtis says the clappers do. Bars marked * are sung low with a guttural, grunting sound. Curtis: any phrase may be repeated, in any order, for an hour or more; this is her written order and proper ending.
N:Guessed (counting bars from the first full bar): the six-in-a-beat groups of bars 12, 13, 26 and 30, written as plain sixteenths and eighths that fill the beat; the five-in-a-beat group of bar 22; the thirty-second-note endings of bars 31-32, approximate; and the underlay of "e" at the end of bar 4 and the start of bar 5. The Chindau spelling wants a Chindau speaker's check.
